title: U.S. Cyclospora Outbreak Expands to Nine States With Nearly 2,000 Taco Bell-Linked Cases
excerpt: The CDC added Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Pennsylvania to the investigation as the largest known cyclosporiasis outbreak in U.S. history now spans nine states, with contaminated iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico identified as the likely source.
body:
• The CDC expanded its cyclosporiasis investigation to nine states after adding Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Pennsylvania, with 1,947 confirmed cases linked to Taco Bell restaurants.
  • Taylor Farms de Mexico recalled all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico on July 17, affecting products shipped to restaurants, retailers, and food service customers in 27 states.
  • More than 4,100 laboratory-confirmed cyclosporiasis cases have been reported across 41 states since May, with Michigan alone accounting for over 8,000 probable cases.
  • Taylor Farms has temporarily shut down its central Mexico processing facility while the FDA and Mexican health authorities continue their investigations.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Friday expanded the largest known cyclosporiasis outbreak in U.S. history to nine states, adding Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Pennsylvania to the five states — Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia — already under investigation.

A total of 1,947 people infected with the Cyclospora parasite who also reported eating at Taco Bell have been identified across the nine states, according to the FDA. At least 98 people have been hospitalized. No deaths have been reported.

“This outbreak may not be limited to the states with known illnesses, and the true number of sick people is likely much higher than the number reported. This is because many people recover without medical care and are not tested for Cyclospora.”

— Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

What Caused the Outbreak

Epidemiological data continues to point to contaminated iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico as the source. The lettuce was distributed by Taylor Farms in California and served at Taco Bell locations across the affected states. Illnesses in the outbreak began on June 22 and have continued through July 20, according to the CDC.

https://x.com/FatherChrisVor1/status/2080697603503821207

On July 17, Taylor Farms initiated a voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico, covering products sold in retail stores, served in restaurants, and distributed to food service customers across 27 states. Taco Bell, owned by Yum Brands, confirmed it had removed all Taylor Farms lettuce from its restaurants.

Taylor Farms is the nation’s largest supplier of lettuce and leafy greens. The company has been linked to previous food safety incidents, including a 2024 E. coli outbreak connected to yellow onions served at some McDonald’s restaurants.

Scale of the Crisis

While the CDC’s confirmed outbreak count stands at 1,947 cases in nine states, the broader picture is far more alarming. More than 4,100 laboratory-confirmed cyclosporiasis cases have been reported across 41 states since May 1, with an additional 7,400 suspected cases, according to the CDC. The agency has cautioned that its case numbers can lag by as much as six weeks behind figures reported by state health officials.

Michigan remains the hardest-hit state by a wide margin. State health officials reported 8,176 probable cases as of Friday — up 532 from the previous day. Michigan health officials have acknowledged that some of their cases may be linked to additional sources beyond the Taylor Farms lettuce, as not every patient interviewed could recall eating lettuce.

Patients in the newly added states likely became ill around the same time as those in the original group but were only recently connected to the same outbreak, according to the Washington Post.

Investigation and Mexico’s Response

The FDA, along with Mexican health authorities, is actively investigating what caused the contamination at Taylor Farms’ central Mexico facility. The company has temporarily shut down the processing plant linked to the outbreak, according to an industry source cited by Reuters.

Mexico’s health ministry pushed back on responsibility, stating on Thursday that its own tests of lettuce and water samples from the Taylor Farms facility came back negative for Cyclospora. Health Minister David Kershenobich denied responsibility for the outbreak on July 21.

The testing challenge is significant. Unlike pathogens such as salmonella or E. coli, Cyclospora cannot be traced using standard genomic sequencing and national databases. Scientists must extract genetic material from the organism and create synthetic DNA copies — a process that can produce false positives. The FDA initially said a sample of Taylor Farms lettuce tested positive for the parasite but later acknowledged the result should be considered a false positive.

What You Need to Know

Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by the parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis, typically spread through food or water contaminated by human fecal matter. Symptoms — including watery diarrhea, cramping, nausea, loss of appetite, and fever — can appear anywhere from two to 14 days after exposure and may persist for weeks without treatment.

The FDA has urged the public to continue avoiding all products listed in Taylor Farms’ recall. For Indian American families in affected states, particularly those in Michigan, Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, and Pennsylvania — home to significant South Asian communities — the recall extends beyond Taco Bell. Taylor Farms supplies iceberg lettuce to multiple restaurant chains and grocery retailers. Checking product labels for Taylor Farms sourcing from central Mexico is advisable until the investigation concludes.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said on July 21 that the outbreak was “under control,” though case numbers have continued to climb since that statement.

What Comes Next

The CDC has said the outbreak may not be limited to the nine states currently identified and is continuing to investigate several other cyclosporiasis clusters that may or may not be linked to the same source. The FDA’s ongoing traceback investigation at Taylor Farms’ Mexico facility will be critical in determining the contamination pathway and preventing future incidents. Seasonal cyclospora infections typically peak between May and August, meaning cases could continue to rise in the coming weeks.
nri_angle: Indian Americans in heavily affected Midwestern and Eastern states should check Taylor Farms recall lists and avoid recalled iceberg lettuce products from central Mexico sold at retailers and restaurants across 27 states.
